⚡ What if the path to universal energy access is not about choosing between grid and off-grid solutions, but planning them together?
 
That question is becoming more urgent. Electricity demand from data centres is set to more than double by 2030, reaching around 945 TWh. In several emerging data-centre hubs, AI infrastructure already accounts for 5 to 20 percent of total electricity demand.
For developing countries, digital growth can crowd in investment and modernise power systems, or compete with households, clinics and small businesses for limited electricity. The outcome depends on how power systems are planned today.
 
New analysis across Burkina Faso, Mali, Nigeria and Senegal shows why this matters. Where grid expansion is constrained, mini-grids can serve between 47 million and 110 million people out of 171 million needing access, accounting for more than half of new connections in some scenarios.
 
Battery storage can strengthen that pathway. Across the scenarios assessed, fuel savings average around US$2 for every US$1 of additional storage investment. Under optimistic mini-grid costs at Tier 2–3 demand levels, savings can reach up to US$4 for every US$1 invested by reducing diesel generation.
 
For me, the lesson is that grid extension, mini-grids, storage and digital infrastructure cannot be planned in isolation. Digital demand is reshaping power-system needs, while grids and storage determine how that growth can be served.
 
For countries still closing their access gaps, the opportunity is to plan grids, storage and digital growth together, so that rising demand expands access and opportunity rather than competing for scarce power.
 
🔗 Further reading: IRENA, Unlocking battery storage potential for sustainable mini-grid electrification in West Africa
